passage: Parveen Khala smiled at her nephew. "Ujjwal, you think you're the first to sulk when your team loses? When I was fifteen, our girls' school was famous for its hockey team. When we won, I walked taller, as if I had scored every goal myself. When we lost the district final, I didn't eat for a day. Then a cousin from another school laughed and said our team was all show. I shouted at her so hard that my Ammi sent me to my room. It felt as if she had insulted me, not a team. Years later I understood: my whole mood lived inside that team. So when your side loses and you feel insulted, check how much of yourself you've handed over."

qa.q: What was Parveen's school famous for?
qa.a: Its hockey team.

qa.q: How did Parveen feel when the cousin laughed at her team?
qa.a: She felt personally insulted, as if the cousin had mocked her rather than just a team.

qa.q: What does Parveen Khala suggest Ujjwal do, and why?
qa.a: To notice how much of himself he has handed over to his team, since she once let her whole mood live inside hers.

qa.q: How might the cousin have seen Parveen's shouting?
qa.a: The cousin may have been taken aback, having meant a light jab about a team, not about Parveen.

grounding: An aunt recalls how as a teenager her mood rose and fell with her school team and an insult to it felt like an insult to her.

passage: Nilesh had a maths exam at nine the next morning and his phone was at eight per cent, but he couldn't put it down. Someone had posted a mocking clip about the band he loved, and Tarun, his own friend, had commented, "Overrated, honestly." Nilesh typed a long reply, deleted it, typed a longer one. His chest was tight, as if Tarun had called him overrated. Last week, when the band won an award, Nilesh had grinned for two days as if he'd won it himself. Now the phone died mid-sentence. In the dark, Nilesh realised he'd done no revision and was furious with a friend over songs. At breakfast Tarun messaged, "Bro you ok? It was just a joke." Nilesh stared at the screen, still stung.

qa.q: What time was Nilesh's maths exam?
qa.a: At nine the next morning.

qa.q: Why did Nilesh's chest feel tight at Tarun's comment?
qa.a: He felt hurt, as if Tarun had called him overrated, because his sense of worth was tied to the band.

qa.q: What could Nilesh try the next time a comment about the band stings?
qa.a: He could put the phone down, remind himself a joke about the band isn't a verdict on him, and talk to Tarun calmly later.

qa.q: How does Tarun seem to see the comment?
qa.a: Tarun sees it as just a joke and seems surprised, checking whether Nilesh is okay.

grounding: A teenager whose mood rises and falls with a band's fortunes feels a friend's criticism of it as a personal insult, even on the night before an exam.

passage: Ujjwal's school had won the city quiz three years running, and he wore the badge on his blazer every day. On Saturday they lost to a school from across town. By Monday Ujjwal was snapping at everyone. When Parveen from the next section said, "Maybe your team got a bit lazy," Ujjwal flushed. "You don't even know what you're talking about," he said, loud enough to stop the corridor. At home he skipped dinner. His mother found him scrolling through old winning photos. "You weren't even on the team, beta." "It's still us," he said. "When they lose, it's like I lost." His mother sat beside him. "And when the school wins, are you a better boy?" Ujjwal didn't answer.

qa.q: How many years running had Ujjwal's school won the city quiz?
qa.a: Three years running.

qa.q: What does Ujjwal mean by 'When they lose, it's like I lost'?
qa.a: His own sense of worth rises and falls with the school's results, so the team's defeat feels personal.

qa.q: What question from his mother could become a turning point, and why?
qa.a: 'When the school wins, are you a better boy?', because it invites Ujjwal to separate his worth from the school's record.

qa.q: How might Parveen have felt when Ujjwal snapped in the corridor?
qa.a: Parveen likely felt embarrassed and surprised at such a strong reaction to a passing comment about the team.

grounding: A teenage boy's mood crashes when his school loses and he defends it fiercely, treating criticism of the team as criticism of him.

passage: "Why's Sahil banging doors?" Mummy asked. Dolma didi didn't look up from her book. "Riverside lost again. Relegated." Sahil stomped in. "It's not funny." "I didn't laugh." "You were going to." He threw himself on the sofa. "Everyone at school will say our city can't even keep a football team." "So?" "So it's us. It's me." Dolma put her book down. "Honestly, their defence has been rubbish all season." "Don't say that!" Sahil sat bolt upright. "You don't even watch them!" "Sahil, I'm talking about eleven players, not you." "It's the same." Mummy sat beside him. "Last month when they won the derby, you were singing in the shower for two days." Sahil said nothing. His ears were red. "You're allowed to love them," Dolma said more gently. "You're just not them."

qa.q: What happened to Riverside, according to Dolma?
qa.a: Riverside lost again and was relegated.

qa.q: Why does Sahil sit bolt upright when Dolma criticises the defence?
qa.a: He feels hurt and defensive, taking the criticism as an attack on himself because he believes the team's loss makes the city, and him, look bad.

qa.q: Which line from Dolma could help Sahil most, and why?
qa.a: 'You're allowed to love them. You're just not them' lets him keep his love for the team while separating his own worth from its results.

qa.q: How does Dolma see Sahil's reaction?
qa.a: She sees him taking a football result as a personal insult, and at first finds it a bit silly, then speaks to him more gently.

grounding: A teenager's mood soars and crashes with his city's football club, and he reacts to criticism of the team as if it were aimed at him.

passage: I'm Ishita. At fifteen, my school's name was stitched into who I was. When the city newspaper ranked us second for board results, I walked about like the proudest girl in the corridor. The next year we slipped to sixth, and my mood slipped with it. I couldn't eat lunch properly. Then someone on an online forum called our school "a rote factory", and I spent till two at night replying to strangers. My friend Pranav, from another school, joked, "Relax, your school isn't your mother." I didn't talk to him for a week. Looking back, what hurt wasn't the ranking. It was that I'd let the school's name hold my own sense of being good enough. I still love my school. I just keep a bit of myself outside it now.

qa.q: Where did someone call Ishita's school 'a rote factory'?
qa.a: Someone called it that on an online forum.

qa.q: Why did Pranav's joke upset Ishita so much at fifteen?
qa.a: Because her sense of being good enough was tied to the school, so a joke about it felt like an insult to her.

qa.q: What turning point helped Ishita keep her pride without being ruled by it?
qa.a: Looking back and seeing that the ranking only hurt because she let the school's name hold her self-worth, she chose to keep part of herself outside it.

qa.q: How might Pranav have felt during the week Ishita didn't talk to him?
qa.a: Pranav might have felt confused and shut out, since he meant a light joke and suddenly lost a friend's company over it.

grounding: A teenager's mood rises and falls with her school's ranking, and she defends it fiercely because insults to the school feel like insults to her.
